title: Deuxième partie : variations sur l'équation des lacets [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois…, pages 293 à 650, dont table des matières] : notes et copies de notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 307-309 of the 'variations sur l'équation des lacets'): Grothendieck is building a purely group-theoretic dictionary for the classical Legendre relation between elliptic curves and rational curves with marked points. The dictionary works with 'loop groups' (discrete fundamental groups with their cusp or loop structure) and the groupoids they form.

Objects and groupoids:
- C^ext_{1,1} is the groupoid of loop groups of type (1,1): fundamental groups of a once-punctured torus, i.e. free groups F2 with the conjugacy class of the commutator loop. Its morphisms are all exterior isomorphisms, including orientation-reversing ones.
- C^ext_{1,1} is connected. Its automorphism group is Autext(π_{1,1}) ≅ GL(2,Z), via the action on the abelianisation (π_{1,1})_ab ≅ Z^2. This is Nielsen's theorem Out(F2) ≅ GL(2,Z), equivalently the extended mapping class group of S_{1,1}.
- So C^ext_{1,1} ≃ Tors(GL(2,Z)).
- C_{0,3} is the analogous groupoid of type (0,3), which I read as the plane minus 3 points: a sphere with 4 punctures, one of them (∞) distinguished. Its exterior automorphism group is the extended mapping class group of S_{0,4} fixing one puncture, B_3/Z(B_3) ⋊ Z/2 ≅ PGL(2,Z).
- This is what 'GP(1,Z)' means: the projective group of P^1 over Z, i.e. PGL(2,Z) = GL(2,Z)/±1.

Previous page: the canonical 'Legendre' functor L: C^ext_{1,1} → C_{0,3} lies over the change-of-groups functor Tors(GL(2,Z)) → Tors(PGL(2,Z)). That functor is not an equivalence, because the central element −id is killed.

This page repairs that:
- −id is an automorphism of every object, natural in the object. It is the hyperelliptic involution, generating the centre {±1} of the fundamental group of the groupoid.
- One forms the quotient groupoid C^ext'_{1,1} by this central universal automorphism. In modern language this is the rigidification (Abramovich–Corti–Vistoli) of the groupoid or stack by the central μ2.
- C^ext'_{1,1} is connected and equivalent to Tors(GL(2,Z)') with GL(2,Z)' = GL(2,Z)/±1.
- The Legendre functor then descends to an equivalence (55) C^ext'_{1,1} ≃ C_{0,3}. It sits in the commutative square (56) over the tautological equivalence Tors(GL(2,Z)') ≃ Tors(GP(1,Z)) induced by the isomorphism (57) GL(2,Z)/±1 ≅ PGL(2,Z).

Geometric meaning: E \ {0} modulo ±1 is A^1 with the three images of the nonzero 2-torsion points marked. This is the topological shadow of M_{1,1} rigidified by μ2 ≅ [M_{0,4}/S_3] (Legendre λ-line). At the level of mapping class groups it is the Birman–Hilden correspondence SL(2,Z)/±1 ≅ Mod(S_{0,4}, ∞) ≅ PSL(2,Z), and its extended version.

Next page: Grothendieck announces that he wants to construct (55) intrinsically, from π_{1,1} and π_{0,3} themselves (starting from the canonical central element of Autext(π'), the 'symmetry' −1), rather than via Teichmüller groups and an ad hoc homomorphism.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. In (56) the left vertical arrow is also an equivalence (both groupoids are connected with matching automorphism groups); this is implicit.
On the previous page 'GP(1,Z) ≃ GL(1,Z)/±1' must be a slip or misreading for GL(2,Z)/±1 = PGL(2,Z); otherwise (57) makes no sense.

The reading of 'type (0,3)' as 'plane minus 3 points, ∞ distinguished' is my interpretation. If C_{0,3} were the groupoid of the thrice-punctured sphere with unmarked cusps, its automorphism group would be finite (S3 × Z/2) and (55) would be false. The equivalence only holds with the 'distinguished fourth point' convention.

ideas.what: Groupoid of type-(1,1) loop groups with all exterior isomorphisms is equivalent to GL(2,Z)-torsors, via the action on the abelianisation
ideas.modern_name: Nielsen's theorem Out(F2) ≅ GL(2,Z); extended mapping class group of the once-punctured torus
ideas.where_published: Teichmüller groupoid ideas appear in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); this specific formulation is not known to me in published texts

ideas.what: Quotienting a groupoid by a universal central automorphism (−id, the hyperelliptic involution)
ideas.modern_name: Rigidification of a stack/gerbe by a central subgroup (μ2-rigidification of M_{1,1})
ideas.where_published: Related banding/gerbe notions are in Giraud's 'Cohomologie non abélienne' (Grothendieck school); this page itself is unpublished

ideas.what: Legendre equivalence C^ext'_{1,1} ≃ C_{0,3} compatible with GL(2,Z)/±1 ≅ PGL(2,Z)
ideas.modern_name: Birman–Hilden correspondence for the elliptic involution; Legendre family, M_{1,1}^{rig} ≅ [M_{0,4}/S_3]-type identification
ideas.usually_credited_to: Legendre/Jacobi (classical); Birman–Hilden (1971–73) for the mapping class group version
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses the M_{0,4}/M_{1,1} Teichmüller groups and their relation (Lego game, levels 1–2), but not this exact groupoid statement

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a clean, correct, but standard step: rigidify the type-(1,1) groupoid by the hyperelliptic centre to get an equivalence with the type-(0,3) groupoid, a Birman–Hilden/Legendre statement. The only mildly interesting element is the announced programme (next page) of constructing this equivalence intrinsically from the loop groups. That programme is not carried out here.
transcription_corrections: In (56) the upper-left object should read C^{ext'}_{1,1} (as in (55)), not C_{1,0}.
'équivalent comme à celui des torseurs' — the 'comme' is probably a residue of 'comme ci-dessus' or a stray word; the sense is 'équivalent à celui des torseurs sous Gl(2,Z)' = Gl(2,Z)/(±1)'.
'Gp(1,Z)' / 'GP(1,Z)' denotes the projective group of P^1 over Z, i.e. PGL(2,Z). The previous page's 'GL(1,Z)/±1' should be 'GL(2,Z)/±1'.
Insertions read correctly: '{±1}' above 'centre', 'groupoïde' above C^ext_{1,1}, 'Gl(2,Z)' =' above the quotient.
